items.title: CVE-2026-68820: Windows WinSock (afd.sys) Use-After-Free Zero-Day Actively Exploited by Lazarus Group in Operation Dream Job
items.summary: Microsoft patched CVE-2026-68820, a use-after-free vulnerability in afd.sys — the Windows Sockets API kernel-mode driver — enabling local privilege escalation to SYSTEM. Confirmed as a zero-day exploited in the wild before patch release. Check Point Research attributes exploitation to North Korea's Lazarus Group, used within Operation Dream Job to elevate privileges on already-compromised systems targeting defense contractors and crypto firms. Part of August 2026 Patch Tuesday which addressed 400+ CVEs.
items.why: Lazarus weaponizing a kernel zero-day in an active, named campaign is high-priority. A SYSTEM-level privilege escalation on any Windows host extends attacker reach to full OS control; patch immediately and hunt for afd.sys exploitation artifacts on any internet-facing or development systems.

items.title: CVE-2026-63520: Microsoft SharePoint Unauthenticated RCE Chain — Actively Exploited Alongside macOS, vCenter, and IKE Flaws
items.summary: CVE-2026-63520, a high-severity SharePoint RCE, chains with a second flaw to create a fully unauthenticated remote code execution path against internet-facing SharePoint deployments. Confirmed actively exploited alongside separate critical flaws in macOS, VMware vCenter, and the Windows IKE stack — all disclosed as part of August 2026 Patch Tuesday. No user interaction required for any of the four attack chains.
items.why: Four concurrently exploited critical flaws across Microsoft, Apple, and VMware platforms signals threat actors are burning 0-days in rapid succession post-Patch-Tuesday. SharePoint RCE without authentication puts any public-facing SharePoint at risk of immediate compromise; organizations should prioritize patching or WAF-blocking SharePoint endpoints today.

items.title: APT-C-60 Targets Japanese Organizations Using GitHub, GitLab, jsDelivr, and Codeberg as C2 Infrastructure
items.summary: APT-C-60, a suspected East Asia-nexus threat group, has continued escalating operations against Japanese organizations throughout 2026 with an evolved TTPs profile. Initial access is achieved via spear-phishing emails delivering RAR archives or Proton Drive links. Post-compromise, the group abuses legitimate developer services — GitHub, GitLab, jsDelivr (CDN), and Codeberg — as command-and-control infrastructure to blend malicious traffic with normal developer activity and evade network-based detection.
items.why: Using mainstream developer platforms as C2 makes traffic indistinguishable from normal developer workflows. Defenders should apply strict egress policy monitoring for GitHub/GitLab API calls from production and endpoint environments — outbound calls to these platforms from non-developer hosts are a red flag requiring investigation.
items.source: OffSeq Threat Radar / Live Threat Intelligence

items.title: CrowdStrike 2026 Annual Threat Hunting Report: AI-Enabled Attacks Surge 89%, eCrime Breakout Time Falls to 29 Minutes
items.summary: CrowdStrike's 2026 Threat Hunting Report documents an 89% year-over-year increase in AI-enabled cyberattacks. Average eCrime breakout time — from initial compromise to lateral movement — has dropped to just 29 minutes. During H1 2026, 88% of CVEs with a public proof-of-concept exploit were weaponized within 48 hours of disclosure, with China-nexus adversaries leading exploitation within the first 24 hours. AI is simultaneously weaponized by attackers for phishing, reconnaissance, and operational scaling, and is increasingly targeted as an enterprise asset.
items.why: A 29-minute mean breakout time leaves no margin for manual SOC investigation — automated, real-time EDR and XDR response is now a baseline requirement. Organizations without sub-5-minute detection-to-containment pipelines are structurally vulnerable to full lateral compromise before human analysts can respond.

items.title: Mandiant M-Trends 2026: Attackers Hand Off Compromised Access in 22 Seconds; Cybercrime and Espionage Groups Diverge Sharply in Tactics
items.summary: Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 report, grounded in 500,000+ hours of frontline incident response investigations conducted globally in 2025, documents that adversaries now hand off compromised initial access to follow-on operators in as little as 22 seconds — effectively eliminating any detection window based on time-to-first-action. The report identifies a sharp tactical divergence: cybercriminal groups optimize for immediate impact and recovery denial (ransomware speed), while sophisticated cyber espionage groups optimize for extreme persistence and minimal footprint. Median global dwell time continues to decline.
items.why: A 22-second access handoff redefines incident response SLAs: initial-access detections must trigger automated containment before human analysts are even paged. The espionage/crime divergence also means defense teams must tune separately for loud-and-fast ransomware versus quiet-and-slow APT operators — a single detection profile covers neither.
